terms.simple_definition: A short-range wireless technology that lets two devices exchange data when they are a few centimetres apart, as in tap-to-pay cards and phone tags.
terms.technical_definition: A set of RFID-derived protocols operating at 13.56 MHz over distances of up to about 10 cm, supporting reader/writer, peer-to-peer and card-emulation modes (ISO/IEC 14443, 18092).
terms.context_example: Users unlock the door by tapping an NFC tag with their phone.

terms.simple_definition: Everyday physical devices, such as sensors, appliances and machines, that are connected to the internet so they can send data and be controlled remotely.
terms.technical_definition: A paradigm in which embedded devices with sensing, actuation and networking capabilities communicate over IP or low-power protocols, typically with cloud or edge services for storage and control.
terms.context_example: Each IoT node reports temperature readings to the server every minute.

terms.simple_definition: A web standard that lets browsers and apps send live audio, video and data directly to each other without plugins.
terms.technical_definition: A set of W3C/IETF APIs and protocols (ICE, STUN/TURN, DTLS-SRTP, SCTP data channels) for peer-to-peer real-time media and data transport between browsers and native clients.
terms.context_example: The camera stream is sent to the user's phone over WebRTC.

terms.simple_definition: A simple text format for storing and sending structured data as named fields and lists, readable by both people and programs.
terms.technical_definition: A language-independent data-interchange format (RFC 8259) built from objects (key/value maps), arrays, strings, numbers, booleans and null.
terms.context_example: The device sends its status as a JSON object.

terms.simple_definition: A square black-and-white pattern that a camera can scan to read a link or a short piece of data.
terms.technical_definition: A two-dimensional matrix barcode (ISO/IEC 18004) encoding up to a few kilobytes of data with Reed–Solomon error correction, read optically by image sensors.
terms.context_example: Visitors scan a QR code to open the registration page.

terms.simple_definition: The basic set of rules that web browsers, apps and servers use to request and send web pages and data.
terms.technical_definition: An application-layer request/response protocol (RFC 9110) in which clients send methods such as GET or POST to resources identified by URLs; HTTPS runs it over TLS.
terms.context_example: The sensor posts its readings to the server over HTTP.

terms.simple_definition: The secure, encrypted version of HTTP used by websites with a padlock in the browser.
terms.technical_definition: HTTP carried over a TLS connection, providing server authentication, confidentiality and integrity for web traffic.
terms.context_example: All API calls are made over HTTPS.

terms.simple_definition: A way for a web server to keep pushing live updates to a browser over one open connection, without the browser asking each time.
terms.technical_definition: A W3C/WHATWG standard (EventSource API) in which the server streams text/event-stream messages to the client over a long-lived HTTP response; communication is one-way, server to client.
terms.context_example: The dashboard receives door events through SSE as soon as they happen.

terms.simple_definition: A trimmed-down version of the Linux operating system that runs inside devices such as routers, smart cameras and single-board computers.
terms.technical_definition: A Linux kernel and user space (often built with Yocto or Buildroot) configured for resource-constrained, application-specific hardware, typically ARM-based boards.
terms.context_example: The gateway runs embedded Linux on a single-board computer.

terms.simple_definition: Technology that uses radio waves to read information from small tags attached to objects, cards or people, without needing to see them.
terms.technical_definition: Automatic identification using a reader that powers and/or interrogates tags over LF, HF (13.56 MHz) or UHF (860–960 MHz) radio links; passive tags harvest energy from the reader's field.
terms.context_example: Each item carries an RFID tag that is read at the gate.

terms.simple_definition: A band of radio frequencies (roughly 300 MHz to 3 GHz) used by TV, mobile phones and long-range RFID tags.
terms.technical_definition: The ITU radio band from 300 MHz to 3 GHz; in RFID, UHF usually refers to the 860–960 MHz band used by EPC Gen2 tags with read ranges of several metres.
terms.context_example: UHF tags can be read from several metres away.

terms.simple_definition: A defined way for one piece of software to ask another for data or actions, like a menu of requests a program can make.
terms.technical_definition: A specification of operations, inputs, outputs and conventions through which software components or services interact, such as a library interface or a web service endpoint set.
terms.context_example: The mobile app calls the server's API to fetch the access log.

terms.simple_definition: A common style for building web APIs where each piece of data has its own web address and is read or changed with standard HTTP requests.
terms.technical_definition: An architectural style for distributed hypermedia systems based on stateless client–server interaction, uniform resource identifiers and standard methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE).
terms.context_example: Door events are stored through a REST endpoint.

terms.simple_definition: A lightweight messaging system that lets small devices publish data to a central server, which forwards it to anyone subscribed.
terms.technical_definition: An OASIS-standard publish/subscribe protocol over TCP in which clients publish to topics on a broker; designed for low bandwidth and unreliable networks, with three quality-of-service levels.
terms.context_example: Sensors publish their readings to an MQTT broker.

terms.simple_definition: A connection that stays open between a browser and a server so both sides can send messages at any time.
terms.technical_definition: A full-duplex protocol (RFC 6455) established through an HTTP upgrade handshake, allowing bidirectional message exchange over a single TCP connection.
terms.context_example: Commands reach the device instantly over a WebSocket.

terms.simple_definition: The core rules the internet uses to address devices and deliver data reliably between them.
terms.technical_definition: The Internet protocol suite: IP provides addressing and packet routing, while TCP adds connection-oriented, ordered and reliable byte-stream delivery with flow and congestion control.
terms.context_example: The reader connects to the server over TCP/IP.

terms.simple_definition: A fast way to send data over a network that does not check whether every piece arrived, often used for live audio and video.
terms.technical_definition: A connectionless transport protocol (RFC 768) sending independent datagrams without delivery, ordering or congestion guarantees.
terms.context_example: Video frames are streamed over UDP to keep latency low.

terms.simple_definition: The encryption layer that keeps data private and tamper-proof while it travels over a network, as used by HTTPS.
terms.technical_definition: A cryptographic protocol (RFC 8446 for TLS 1.3) providing authenticated key exchange, confidentiality and integrity for connections; successor to SSL.
terms.context_example: All traffic between the gateway and the cloud is protected with TLS.

terms.simple_definition: Scrambling data with a secret key so that only someone with the right key can read it.
terms.technical_definition: The transformation of plaintext into ciphertext using a cryptographic algorithm and key, so that recovering the plaintext without the decryption key is computationally infeasible.
terms.context_example: Medical data are encrypted before being uploaded.

terms.simple_definition: A widely used method for encrypting data with a shared secret key.
terms.technical_definition: A symmetric block cipher (FIPS 197) with a 128-bit block and 128-, 192- or 256-bit keys, based on the Rijndael substitution–permutation network.
terms.context_example: Stored records are protected with AES-256.

terms.simple_definition: A classic public-key encryption method where anyone can encrypt with a public key but only the owner of the private key can decrypt.
terms.technical_definition: A public-key cryptosystem whose security rests on the difficulty of factoring the product of two large primes; used for encryption and digital signatures.
terms.context_example: Session keys are exchanged using RSA.

terms.simple_definition: Encryption that uses a pair of keys: a public one anyone can use to lock data, and a private one only the owner can use to unlock it.
terms.technical_definition: Cryptographic schemes based on key pairs in which the public key can be distributed openly, enabling encryption to a recipient and verification of signatures made with the private key.
terms.context_example: Each device holds a key pair for public-key cryptography.

terms.simple_definition: A form of public-key encryption that gives strong security with much shorter keys, which suits small devices.
terms.technical_definition: Public-key cryptography based on the algebraic structure of elliptic curves over finite fields, whose security relies on the elliptic-curve discrete logarithm problem.
terms.context_example: ECC keys are used because the sensor has little memory.

terms.simple_definition: Encryption where data can only be opened by people whose attributes (such as role or department) match a rule set by the data owner.
terms.technical_definition: A public-key scheme in which ciphertexts and keys are associated with attributes and access policies, so decryption succeeds only if a user's attributes satisfy the policy.
terms.context_example: With ABE, only medical staff can decrypt the shared file.

terms.simple_definition: A calculation that turns any data into a short fixed-length fingerprint; changing the data even slightly changes the fingerprint completely.
terms.technical_definition: A function mapping arbitrary-length input to a fixed-length digest; cryptographic hash functions (e.g. SHA-256) are preimage-, second-preimage- and collision-resistant.
terms.context_example: Passwords are stored as the output of a hash function.

terms.simple_definition: Checking that a user or device really is who it claims to be, for example with a password, key card or fingerprint.
terms.technical_definition: The process of verifying the identity of a principal using one or more factors (knowledge, possession, inherence), distinct from authorization, which decides what that principal may do.
terms.context_example: Users pass two-factor authentication before the door opens.

terms.simple_definition: Rules that decide who is allowed to see or use a resource, such as a file, system or room.
terms.technical_definition: Mechanisms and policies (e.g. role-based or attribute-based models) that grant or deny authenticated subjects permission to perform operations on objects.
terms.context_example: Access control rules are stored on the server.

terms.simple_definition: Using computers, storage and software run by a provider over the internet instead of on your own machines.
terms.technical_definition: On-demand network access to a shared pool of configurable computing resources (servers, storage, applications) that can be provisioned rapidly, as defined by NIST SP 800-145.
terms.context_example: Measurements are archived in cloud storage.

terms.simple_definition: Processing data close to where it is produced, on or near the device, instead of sending everything to a distant data centre.
terms.technical_definition: A distributed computing model placing computation and storage at or near data sources (gateways, base stations, devices) to reduce latency, bandwidth use and dependence on the cloud.
terms.context_example: Faces are recognised by edge computing on the camera itself.

terms.simple_definition: A small computer built into a larger device to do one specific job, like the controller inside a washing machine or a smart lock.
terms.technical_definition: A dedicated computing system, usually based on a microcontroller or system-on-chip, integrated into a device to perform specific control or processing functions under real-time and resource constraints.
terms.context_example: The lock is driven by an embedded system with a Wi-Fi module.

terms.simple_definition: A tiny, cheap computer on a single chip that controls electronics such as sensors, motors and lights.
terms.technical_definition: An integrated circuit combining a processor core, memory (flash, RAM) and programmable peripherals (GPIO, ADC, timers, serial interfaces) for embedded control.
terms.context_example: A microcontroller reads the sensor every second.

terms.simple_definition: The software permanently stored on a device's chip that controls how its hardware works.
terms.technical_definition: Low-level software held in non-volatile memory that initialises and controls device hardware; may be updated in the field (over-the-air updates).
terms.context_example: The reader's firmware was updated to support the new tags.

terms.simple_definition: A low-cost, credit-card-sized computer often used for prototypes, teaching and home projects.
terms.technical_definition: A family of ARM-based single-board computers that typically run Linux and expose GPIO pins for connecting sensors and peripherals.
terms.context_example: The gateway prototype runs on a Raspberry Pi.

terms.simple_definition: An easy-to-use electronics board and programming tool for building simple devices that sense and control things.
terms.technical_definition: An open-source hardware and software platform of microcontroller boards (e.g. AVR, ARM) programmed in a C++ dialect through the Arduino IDE.
terms.context_example: An Arduino controls the relay that opens the lock.

terms.simple_definition: A popular low-cost chip with built-in Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, widely used in smart-home and IoT devices.
terms.technical_definition: A family of Espressif system-on-chip microcontrollers with integrated 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi and Bluetooth/BLE radios, commonly programmed with ESP-IDF or Arduino.
terms.context_example: Each node uses an ESP32 to send data over Wi-Fi.

terms.simple_definition: A version of Bluetooth that uses very little power, used by fitness trackers, beacons and smart locks.
terms.technical_definition: The low-power Bluetooth radio specification (since Bluetooth 4.0) operating at 2.4 GHz, optimised for short bursts of data with long battery life.
terms.context_example: The tag advertises its ID over BLE.

terms.simple_definition: The common wireless technology that connects phones, laptops and devices to a local network and the internet.
terms.technical_definition: Wireless local-area networking based on the IEEE 802.11 family of standards, operating mainly in the 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz bands.
terms.context_example: The camera connects to the home router over Wi-Fi.

terms.simple_definition: A low-power wireless network standard used by smart-home devices such as bulbs and sensors to talk to each other.
terms.technical_definition: A mesh networking specification built on IEEE 802.15.4, designed for low data rate, low power wireless sensor and control networks.
terms.context_example: Sensors join a Zigbee mesh around the house.

terms.simple_definition: A long-range, low-power radio technology that lets sensors send small amounts of data over several kilometres.
terms.technical_definition: A chirp spread-spectrum modulation for sub-GHz bands; LoRaWAN is the MAC-layer protocol defining star-of-stars networks with gateways and a network server.
terms.context_example: Field sensors report soil moisture over LoRa.

terms.simple_definition: A component that measures something in the physical world, such as temperature, light or motion, and turns it into a signal a computer can read.
terms.technical_definition: A transducer that converts a physical, chemical or biological quantity into an electrical signal, characterised by sensitivity, range, resolution and noise.
terms.context_example: A temperature sensor is mounted near the skin.

terms.simple_definition: A part that makes something move or change, such as a motor, valve or electric lock, when it receives a signal.
terms.technical_definition: A device that converts a control signal into physical action (motion, force, flow), e.g. motors, solenoids and relays.
terms.context_example: The actuator releases the latch when access is granted.

terms.simple_definition: The delay between something being sent or requested and it arriving or happening.
terms.technical_definition: The time interval between a stimulus and the response, e.g. the end-to-end delay of a message across a network, typically measured in milliseconds.
terms.context_example: Video latency stayed below 200 ms.

terms.simple_definition: How much data or work a system actually gets through in a given time.
terms.technical_definition: The rate of successful data delivery or task completion per unit time (e.g. bits per second, requests per second), bounded by bandwidth and protocol overhead.
terms.context_example: Throughput dropped when twenty clients were connected.

terms.simple_definition: The maximum amount of data a connection can carry per second.
terms.technical_definition: In networking, the maximum data rate of a link (bits per second); in signal processing, the width of the frequency range a signal or channel occupies.
terms.context_example: Compressing the images saves bandwidth.

terms.simple_definition: Devices talking directly to each other instead of going through a central server.
terms.technical_definition: A network architecture in which nodes act as both clients and servers, exchanging data directly rather than via a central coordinator.
terms.context_example: The call is set up peer-to-peer once both devices are found.

terms.simple_definition: Software that sits between applications and the system or network, handling shared jobs such as messaging, security or data exchange.
terms.technical_definition: A software layer providing common services (communication, authentication, data management) to distributed applications beyond those of the operating system.
terms.context_example: A middleware layer translates sensor data into a common format.

terms.simple_definition: An organised store of data that software can search, update and keep safe.
terms.technical_definition: A structured collection of data managed by a database management system (relational/SQL or NoSQL) providing querying, indexing, transactions and concurrency control.
terms.context_example: Every access event is written to a database.

terms.simple_definition: The standard language for asking questions of, and making changes to, data stored in tables.
terms.technical_definition: A declarative language (ISO/IEC 9075) for defining, querying and manipulating data in relational database systems.
terms.context_example: The logs are queried with SQL.

terms.simple_definition: Teaching computers to spot patterns and make predictions from examples, instead of programming every rule by hand.
terms.technical_definition: The study of algorithms that improve performance on a task through experience (data), including supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning.
terms.context_example: A machine learning model flags unusual access patterns.

terms.simple_definition: A computer model made of many simple connected units, loosely inspired by the brain, that learns patterns from data.
terms.technical_definition: A parameterised function composed of layers of weighted linear transformations and non-linear activations, trained by gradient-based optimisation such as backpropagation.
terms.context_example: A small neural network classifies the sensor signal.

terms.simple_definition: Machine learning with large neural networks that have many layers, used for tasks like recognising images and speech.
terms.technical_definition: A subfield of machine learning using multi-layer (deep) neural networks to learn hierarchical representations directly from raw data.
terms.context_example: Deep learning is used to recognise visitors' faces.

terms.simple_definition: A type of neural network designed for images, which looks at small patches at a time to find edges, shapes and objects.
terms.technical_definition: A neural network that uses convolutional layers with shared, spatially local filters (plus pooling and non-linearities) to learn translation-equivariant features from grid-like data.
terms.context_example: A CNN detects people in the camera image.

terms.simple_definition: A processor with thousands of small cores that can do many calculations at once, used for graphics and for training AI models.
terms.technical_definition: A massively parallel processor optimised for throughput on data-parallel workloads (graphics, linear algebra), programmed via APIs such as CUDA or OpenCL.
terms.context_example: Training took two days on eight GPUs.

terms.simple_definition: A chip whose internal circuits can be rewired after manufacturing, so engineers can build custom hardware without making a new chip.
terms.technical_definition: An integrated circuit of configurable logic blocks and programmable interconnects, configured with a hardware description language such as VHDL or Verilog.
terms.context_example: The signal processing runs on an FPGA.

terms.simple_definition: A shared record of transactions kept by many computers, where each new entry is chained to the previous ones so past entries are very hard to change.
terms.technical_definition: An append-only distributed ledger of cryptographically linked blocks, maintained by a peer-to-peer network that agrees on its state through a consensus protocol.
terms.context_example: Access logs are anchored to a blockchain for auditing.

terms.simple_definition: A standard way of formatting and exchanging medical records so different healthcare systems can understand each other.
terms.technical_definition: An HL7 standard defining modular data 'resources' (e.g. Patient, Observation) and a RESTful API for exchanging electronic health information.
terms.context_example: Sensor readings are stored as FHIR Observation resources.

terms.simple_definition: Automatic cleanup in which a program's runtime frees memory that is no longer being used.
terms.technical_definition: Automatic memory management in which the runtime identifies unreachable objects (e.g. by tracing or reference counting) and reclaims their memory.
terms.context_example: Java frees unused objects through garbage collection.

terms.simple_definition: The area of a program's memory used for data created while it runs, whose size isn't known in advance.
terms.technical_definition: A region of process memory for dynamic allocation, managed explicitly (malloc/free) or by a garbage collector, as opposed to the call stack.
terms.context_example: Objects created at run time are stored in heap memory.

terms.simple_definition: A technique that lets a model weigh how much each word (or item) in a sequence matters to every other one when building its understanding.
terms.technical_definition: An operation computing each position's output as a weighted sum of value vectors, with weights from scaled dot products of query and key vectors across all positions of the same sequence.
terms.context_example: The Transformer relies entirely on self-attention.
